opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That question gets right at the heart of what excites me.

When we talk about an agent learning about the world through its own predictions, the basic idea is that knowledge doesn't have to be handed to the system as labels, facts, or a model someone else built. Instead, the agent can build up its understanding by continually asking and answering questions about its own future experience. Something like: "If I keep doing what I'm doing, how much will this sensor reading change over the next few seconds?" Or: "If I reach out my hand, will I feel pressure?" Each of those is a prediction grounded entirely in the agent's own stream of sensation and action.

That's what I mean by its own frame of reference. The predictions aren't about some abstract, objective description of the world. They're about what *this* agent will see, feel, and experience given what *it* does. In reinforcement learning we formalize this using what Rich Sutton and others called general value functions. A standard value function predicts future reward. A general value function predicts the accumulation of any signal the agent cares about, under a particular way of behaving, over a particular time horizon. Once you have that tool, you can ask thousands of these little questions in parallel and learn the answers online, from moment to moment, as the agent interacts with the world.

What's powerful is that this knowledge is verifiable by the agent itself. If it predicts that the room will get darker when it turns left, it can turn left and check. It doesn't need a human teacher to say whether it was right. That makes the learning scalable and continual, and the knowledge stays tied to things that actually matter for the agent's behavior.

A lot of my work has been in prosthetics and rehabilitation, and this is where it becomes very concrete. Imagine a robotic arm attached to a person. We can't hand-specify everything about how that particular person moves, how their muscle signals change when they're tired, or what they're about to try to do. But the arm can learn to predict things like "which joint will the user want to move next?" or "where will my gripper be in half a second?" Those predictions then let the device anticipate, adapt, and make control smoother and more intuitive. The device builds an understanding of its partner and its environment from the inside out.

So, for me, predictive knowledge from the agent's own perspective is a foundation. It's a way for an agent to construct a rich, grounded model of its world, one question at a time, and keep updating it for as long as it lives and acts. I think that's a big part of how we'll get to systems that are truly adaptive and that can work closely with people.

r001.rationale: It describes understanding the world through predictions of what this agent will sense given what it does, with examples such as reaching and turning.

r002.rationale: It explains that an agent can act, such as reaching or turning, and learn by checking how those actions affect its sensory experience.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that predictions about movement give rise to a subjective feeling of agency.

r004.rationale: It does not state that prediction comes before motor control.

r005.rationale: It discusses predictions of future experience and agent-verifiable learning, but does not claim that reward signals and raw sensorimotor predictions suffice for everything the agent needs to know about the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, an agent, whether that's a robot, a piece of software, or a person, only ever has access to its own stream of experience. It gets sensations coming in, it takes actions, and that's it. It doesn't have some privileged God's-eye view of the world handed to it. So if it's going to build up knowledge about the world, that knowledge has to be grounded in the only thing it actually has, which is that stream of sensorimotor data.

And the idea that I find really compelling, and this comes a lot out of the work Rich Sutton and others at Alberta have been doing for years, is that a huge amount of what we'd call knowledge can be expressed as predictions. Not predictions about some abstract state of the world, but predictions about the agent's own future experience. If I do this, what will I feel? If I keep walking down this hallway, how long until I hit a wall? What will my sensors read in half a second?

The beautiful thing about framing knowledge that way is that it's verifiable from inside the agent. The agent makes a prediction, time passes, and it either sees the thing it predicted or it doesn't. It doesn't need a human to come in and label anything. It can just compare what it expected to what actually happened and update. That's what makes it continual learning in the real sense. You're never done, you're always checking your predictions against the world as it unfolds.

And you can layer these predictions. Once you have one prediction, that prediction itself becomes a signal you can predict about. So you start to get this web of predictive knowledge where some predictions are very close to raw sensation and others are quite abstract, but they're all still anchored to the agent's own experience. That's where the frame-of-reference piece matters to me. The agent isn't learning "the truth about the world." It's learning what the world is like for it, given its body and its sensors and the things it can do. For a prosthetic limb, which is a lot of what I work on, that turns out to be exactly what you want. The device doesn't need to know what a cup is in some objective sense. It needs to predict what the person is about to do and what its own sensors are about to report so it can be helpful in that moment.

r001.rationale: The response frames knowledge about the world as predictions about the agent’s future experience, including what it will sense after taking an action.

r002.rationale: It mentions actions and comparing predictions with later experience, but does not explain that exploratory movements teach the agent how actions change its sensory experience.

r003.rationale: It does not connect predictions about movement to a subjective feeling of agency.

r004.rationale: It does not state that prediction precedes motor control.

r005.rationale: It discusses predictive knowledge but does not say that reward signals and predictions of raw sensorimotor experience suffice to learn everything needed about the world.

astra-6.text:
I think the key idea is that an agent can understand its world in terms of what it expects to experience. Rather than starting with a description of the world that someone else has supplied, it can ask: What signals will I receive next? What will happen if I take this action? And how might those signals change over a longer period of time?

Imagine reaching for a cup. You might predict what you’ll see as your hand moves, when you’ll feel contact, and how much pressure you’ll need to keep the cup from slipping. Those predictions are grounded in your own interaction with the cup. And when they’re wrong, that gives you an opportunity to learn.

What’s interesting is that this gives us a way to think about knowledge as something an agent can continually test against its experience. It doesn’t need to have a complete model of everything in the world. It needs predictions that help it make sense of what’s happening and choose what to do next.

r001.rationale: The response frames understanding through predictions about what the agent will sense during actions, illustrated by reaching for and handling a cup.

r002.rationale: It says prediction errors create an opportunity to learn, but does not clearly explain exploratory movements as a way to learn how actions change sensory experience.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect predictions about movement to a subjective feeling of agency.

r004.rationale: It does not state that prediction occurs before motor control.

r005.rationale: It does not mention reward signals or claim that raw sensorimotor predictions suffice for learning everything about the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of prediction as a way for an agent to connect its experience to what might happen next. From the agent’s perspective, it has a stream of sensations and actions. It can ask, “Given what I’m sensing now, and if I behave in a particular way, what should I expect to experience?”

Those predictions can be very immediate—what will I feel if I move my hand?—or extend over longer periods. And they don’t have to be predictions about a single next observation. They might be about how much of something the agent will encounter over time.

What’s useful is that the agent can check those expectations against its own experience. It makes a prediction, acts, observes what happens, and updates. So you get a notion of knowledge that is grounded in the agent’s interaction with the world, and that can continually change as the agent learns.

r001.rationale: The response describes predicting future experience based on sensing and acting, but does not characterize objects themselves as predictions about interaction outcomes.

r002.rationale: It mentions acting, observing, and updating, but does not explain that exploratory movements teach how actions change sensory experience.

r003.rationale: It does not connect predictions about movement to the subjective feeling of agency.

r004.rationale: It does not state that prediction precedes motor control.

r005.rationale: It does not propose that reward signals and raw sensorimotor predictions suffice to learn everything needed about the world.
